Return Seminar: Valorization of Tamarind Seed By-Products: Carbon Dot–Reinforced Xyloglucan Nanocomposite Films

Abstract:

More than 0.3 billion tons of plastic are produced globally each year, most of which is derived from non-renewable resources and is non-biodegradable, leading to its persistent accumulation in the environment and significantly contributing to the generation of microplastics and nanoplastics. The development of sustainable and functional food packaging materials from renewable resources has gained significant attention as an eco-friendly alternative to petroleum-based plastics. In this context, tamarind seed represents a valuable and underutilized biomass resource rich in xyloglucan (XG), a naturally occurring hemicellulosic polysaccharide with excellent film-forming ability. Xyloglucan consists of a β-(1→4)-linked D-glucan backbone, structurally similar to cellulose, substituted with α-(1→6)-linked xylose side chains that may further carry galactose residues. This branched molecular architecture provides high water affinity, strong hydrogen-bonding capability, and good flexibility. Given that India is the world’s largest producer of tamarind, this study explores tamarind kernel–derived xyloglucan as a biopolymeric matrix for the fabrication of multifunctional nanocomposite films. To enhance the functional performance of XG films, carbon dots (CDs) were synthesized from tamarind seed coat biomass and incorporated into the XG matrix at concentrations ranging from 1 to 5% (w/w). The CDs, rich in oxygen-containing surface functional groups such as hydroxyl, carboxyl, and carbonyl moieties, were characterized using fluorescence spectroscopy. The influence of CD loading on the rheological behavior of film-forming solutions and the structural, mechanical, barrier, optical, and functional properties of the resulting films was systematically investigated. Rheological measurements revealed non-Newtonian shear-thinning behavior of the XG/CD film-forming solutions, attributable to polymer chain entanglement and alignment under applied shear. Incorporation of CDs significantly enhanced intermolecular interactions through hydrogen bonding between the surface functional groups of the CDs and the hydroxyl-rich XG polymer chains, as confirmed by FTIR and XRD analyses. These interactions resulted in improved structural integrity and overall film performance. Among all formulations, the XG/CD film containing 4% CDs exhibited the most balanced and superior properties, including enhanced tensile strength (8.34±0.89 MPa) and elastic modulus (156.96±22.01 MPa), reduced water vapor permeability (2.59±0.29×10⁻¹¹ g·m/m²·s·Pa), increased surface hydrophobicity (88.07±2.97°), improved UV-blocking capability, and notable antioxidant activity (88.68±0.58% DPPH inhibition). The films also demonstrated antimicrobial activity against E. coli and B. subtilis. At higher CD loading (5%), slight nanoparticle agglomeration was observed, which negatively affected film uniformity and functional properties. Overall, this study demonstrates that optimized XG/CD4% nanocomposite film shows strong potential as an eco-friendly, active food packaging material capable of extending shelf life and improving food safety. Keywords: Tamarind kernel xyloglucan; Carbon dots; Biopolymer nanocomposites, Active food packaging; Waste valorization
